newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium to head higher as deficit rises - MBR.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium to head higher as deficit rises - MBR.

text.p: Aluminium prices are expected to rise sharply from 1998 as the market supply deficit increases from a forecast 230,000 tonnes in 1997, according to industry analyst Metal Bulletin Research (MBR).
Average spot prices are seen rising from $1,620 per tonne this year to $1,800 per tonne and $2,250 per tonne in 1998 and 1999 respectively, peaking at over $2,300.

"We are forecasting a metal deficit of approximately 230,000 tonnes during 1997, and increasing deficits over 1998 and 1999, when we do expect prices to reflect the more bullish market conditions," MBR said.
Fund buying will come into play before supplies start to tighten, also helping to boost prices, it added.

The rapid drawdown in producer and exchange stocks in recent months has been underpinned by strong demand for aluminium semis and western world consumption is seen rising by 4.6% to 18.3m tonnes in 1997, MBR said.
In 1998-2000, demand is expected to grow more slowly, by 1.5-3% as destocking becomes a factor and the packaging market reaches maturity.
"With continued growth expected in the emerging economies, our consumption forecasts of 2.6% and 1.7% in 1999 and 2000 can be viewed as conservative," the analyst said.

This compares with a 3.8% increase in production to 16.152m tonnes this year, followed by increases of 5.1% in 1998 and 3% and 3.1% in 1999 and 2000 respectively, when a supply bottleneck is expected.
Net east-west trade, which has helped ease the growing deficit, is seen falling to 1.62m tonnes by 2000, from 2.16m tonnes this year.
CIS consumption is expected to rise sharply from its current low base and Hungary's increased importance in value-added production will reduce the flow of material to the west, MBR said.

"Although Chinese production should continue to grow strongly in the years 1997-2001, much of the increase is likely to be absorbed by the mass expansion in the country's downstream sector," the analyst added.
Aluminium prices have been disappointing recently because of rumours of a hidden stock build up, overstocking in the downstream industries and idled capacity, MBR said.

"Nevertheless, in our opinion the outlook for the metal remains strong, and we believe that prices will move gradually higher during the second half of the year to reflect the fundamentals," it added.
